source.title: Low Rank and Sparse Fourier Structure in Recurrent Networks Trained on Modular Addition

record.tranche_reason: Extends mechanistic analysis of modular-addition networks to a vanilla RNN and reports results on its generalization and learned Fourier structure.
record.gate_note: The paper reports one test-loss checkpoint but does not report training accuracy or a test-accuracy trajectory. Its Fourier analyses and ablations characterize the final solution; they do not measure how the circuit forms over training. The cited grokking results are not counted.
record.test_reason: Trains a vanilla RNN, a new architecture, on the original mod-113 addition task. Its own analyses show the same Fourier multiplication algorithm reported for one-layer transformers, and it reports that this algorithm recurs across several training runs and data fractions. This bears on V6. It reports no training-accuracy curve, delay, or circuit formation over training, so V1, V2 and V5 are not tested.
record.authors_conclusion: Largely correct. The authors conclude that RNNs trained on modular addition learn the Fourier multiplication algorithm also found in one-layer transformers and MLPs. They find the solution is low rank and sparse in Fourier space, with unembedding singular-vector pairs tied to specific frequencies, and frequencies causally needed in aggregate. They report the same structure across runs and data fractions of 30-70%.
record.recipe_differences: Uses Fourier-domain analysis and frequency ablations inspired by prior modular-addition interpretability work, but applies them to a vanilla RNN and adds low-rank weight analysis; it does not reproduce the original grokking time-course measurements.
record.method_sensitivity: The number of significant Fourier frequencies varies between 6 and 8 across the reported training runs and data fractions.

fits_no_version.finding: The RNN's weights are low rank (r=12, or 32 for Whh), and rank equals twice the number of frequencies. Ablating single frequencies leaves accuracy at ≥99.4%, while cumulative ablation drops it to chance.
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: Modular-addition networks learn a low-rank solution that is sparse in Fourier space and redundant across frequencies, with frequency components causally necessary in aggregate.

record.peer_reviewed: IEEE International Conference on Acoustics, Speech, and Signal Processing
record.problems: The grokking evidence is limited to a reported test-loss endpoint: training accuracy, the earlier test-accuracy trajectory, and delay-versus-data-size results are not given. The repeated-run summary does not enumerate runs or individual outcomes. Several Fourier spectra are presented in figures rather than tabulated.

untested.parts: All of it. There is no training-accuracy saturation, test-accuracy trajectory, delay, or delay-versus-training-set-size result; only a test-loss endpoint.
Circuit formation over training, removal of memorizing components, and progress measures anticipating the jump. Only the final model is analyzed.
Non-algorithmic data and initialization-scale or weight-norm manipulation.
Weight decay is fixed. There is no efficiency comparison, critical dataset size, or ungrokking.
Hyperparameters other than data fraction are not varied. Other recurrent architectures (e.g. S4 or Mamba) are not tested. The number of runs per fraction is not stated.
Optimizer and floating-point or softmax artifacts.

missing.what: In WE, Wih and Whh there is no one-to-one mapping between singular vectors and frequencies; ablating one frequency also affects other components. This qualifies how cleanly the algorithm is identifiable outside the unembedding layer.

record.verdict_notes: Neither original source is this paper. The test-loss endpoint is setup information, not a grokking measurement. V6 support is modest: one architecture plus an aggregate, unenumerated replication statement, with no uncertainty reported. The frequency set varying across runs is consistent with Nanda et al. and does not imply a different algorithm.

versions.untested_parts: The paper does not report training accuracy saturation, chance-level test accuracy before generalization, or how the delay changes with training-set size.

The paper analyzes the final Fourier solution and ablates frequencies, but does not track circuit formation, removal of memorizing components, or whether progress measures anticipate a generalization jump.
No non-algorithmic data, initialization-scale or weight-norm transition is tested.
No LLM or realistic-data pretraining or fine-tuning is studied.
Weight decay is used in training, but the paper does not test an efficiency account, critical dataset size, or ungrokking.
The comparison is across training runs and data fractions for the same RNN setup; architecture and hyperparameters are not varied.
The paper does not test adaptive-optimizer instabilities or floating-point/softmax artifacts.

rows.subject: single-layer vanilla RNN
rows.operation_detail: Train on modular addition modulo 113 for 20,000 epochs
rows.value: zero test loss after around 4000 epochs
rows.note: No training-accuracy value or test trajectory is reported, so this result alone does not establish the claimed delay from training saturation or a chance-to-near-perfect transition.
rows.check: A single test-loss endpoint (zero after ~4000 epochs) with no training-accuracy curve. It cannot show a delay after training saturation or a chance-to-perfect jump, so it should not be linked to V1.

rows.subject: RNNs across training runs (aggregate; number of runs not stated)
rows.size_stated: state size 256 for the described setup
rows.operation_detail: Compare learned Fourier spectra and low-rank structure across training runs and data fractions
rows.measure: consistency of low-rank structure and sparse Fourier spectra
rows.value: The paper reports the same low-rank structure and sparse Fourier spectra in all cases; significant Fourier frequencies varied between 6 and 8.
rows.note: Aggregate report across runs; individual runs and their frequency sets are not enumerated. The shared structure supports a common Fourier-solution family, while the frequency count varies.
rows.check: The same low-rank, sparse-Fourier solution appears in all runs from 30% to 70% data. The frequency count varies (6-8), and Wfc rank is always twice that count. This is the same algorithm with different frequency choices, so observed rather than partial.

rows.subject: single-layer vanilla RNN
rows.operation_detail: Analyze Fourier coefficients at nodes in the computational graph
rows.measure: dominant Fourier frequencies across embedding, unembedding, and hidden-state signals
rows.value: Most energy is in frequencies k ∈ {6, 15, 20, 29, 47, 54}; the same six dominant frequencies appear across the analyzed signals.
rows.note: The text describes the dominant-frequency finding; the plotted coefficients are not tabulated.
rows.check: The RNN's sparse Fourier representation, with the same six frequencies at every node, matches the transformer algorithm in Nanda et al. This is cross-architecture evidence that bears on V6.

relationships.condition: Vanilla tanh RNN on mod-113 addition, compared with prior one-layer transformer results and across runs at 30-70% data
relationships.reason: The RNN uses the same Fourier multiplication algorithm: sparse frequencies at all nodes (r3) and cos/sin(ωk(a+b)) fits with error ≲1e-2 (r9-r14). The same structure appears in all runs (r2). Only the number of frequencies (6-8) and the readability of singular vectors vary.
relationships.display_finding: All runs showed sparse Fourier multiplication structure with sine and cosine fit errors ≲10⁻², while the number of frequencies ranged from 6 to 8 and singular-vector readability varied.
